Escalations & vetoes

5-minute walkthrough (click order)
  1. Live, cascade, 30 fps (1 min). Most frames take the fast path at 128 px; the orange badge appears only when the margin drops below the threshold. Point at RSS: about 200 MB for the whole inference process.
  2. Switch to 60 fps, then turn on the deadline toggle (45 s). The deadline shrinks to 16.7 ms and red vetoes appear: the system gives up some accuracy to stay on time.
  3. Switch to INT8-dyn 224 px (30 s). No escalations and a tighter p99, but a higher p50. That's the tail-vs-median trade.
  4. Phase 1 tab (1 min). My hypothesis was wrong: k-center calibration lost to random. But the margin signal (AUROC 0.879) became the basis for everything after.
  5. Phase 2 tab (1 min). Routing's p99 was bad because the GPU goes cold between sparse escalations (8.8 → ~23 ms). FP16 on every frame won on the GPU, but that process uses about 1 GB.
  6. Phase 3 tab (1 min). The scatter: about 5× less RAM than the torch + MPS router at equal or better accuracy. Then the four techniques, one sentence each.
  7. Back to Live (spare time). Webcam, or the probe config, which is clearly labeled because it uses labels.
Talking points: Live
  • This is the Phase 3 pipeline running live: one INT8 ONNX session, numpy preprocessing, CPU only. The inference worker never imports torch, so the RSS number is honest.
  • Number to emphasize: about 200 MB for the whole inference process, versus about 1,010 MB for the torch + MPS router from Phase 2.
  • The cascade runs every frame at 128 px (17 tokens, about 5 ms). When the margin is below a threshold set on train margins, it re-runs the same weights at 224 px. About 22–25% of frames re-run.
  • The deadline veto skips the second pass if a frame is already queued or the pass would miss the deadline. At 30 fps it rarely fires; at 60 fps it does.
  • These are live numbers on a shared laptop running a browser and screen share. The offline numbers came from isolated processes with 3 repeats under caffeinate, which is why both are shown.
Likely question: "Why does the webcam do worse than CIFAR?"
Answer: I downsample webcam frames to 32×32 so they go through exactly the same pipeline as CIFAR, so it's a domain shift. I don't claim real-world accuracy; native-resolution frames would also gain less from the 128 px path.

Phase 1: coverage-based calibration doesn't help measured offline

Top-1 accuracy vs calibration size

Source: results/accuracy_vs_N.png · full 10,000-image test set · static INT8 QDQ on ORT CPU

What happened

  • Hypothesis: picking calibration images to cover CLIP's embedding space (greedy k-center) beats random selection for static INT8, especially at small N.
  • Result: no. K-center was never better than random beyond seed noise, and it was clearly worse at N=512.
  • Best explanation: farthest-point sampling picks outliers on purpose. MinMax calibration stretches activation ranges to cover them, which coarsens the quantization step for typical images.

The finding that carried forward: confidence routing

Source: results/routing_auroc.json, results/routing_e2e.json

Offline routing sweep: INT8 first, escalate low-margin images

Source: results/routing.csv · latencies composed from per-image batch-1 timings (the end-to-end check showed this p99 is optimistic)
Talking points: Phase 1
  • I started with a clean hypothesis, and it was wrong. I report it as a negative result rather than tuning until something worked.
  • Number to emphasize: 84.26% vs 85.68% at N=512 (k-center vs random mean; random seeds span 85.58–85.81%).
  • K-center did achieve its objective (coverage radius 0.54 vs about 0.65 for random). Coverage is simply the wrong target for MinMax: range-representative samples matter more.
  • The useful by-product: the INT8 top-1/top-2 margin flags INT8 ≠ FP32 disagreements with AUROC 0.879, versus 0.604 for distance to the calibration set.
  • The composed routing estimate said 22.7 ms p99, but a real end-to-end run measured 33.9 ms. That gap started Phase 2.
Likely question: "Would k-center work with a different calibrator?"
Answer: Possibly. Percentile or entropy calibration is less sensitive to outliers, so that's the first follow-up. I only tested MinMax and say so in the README.

Phase 2: the tail came from a cold GPU measured offline

FP16 batch-1 latency on MPS: back-to-back vs after idle

Why routing lost

  • Why the tail was bad: routing sends the GPU only about 10% of frames, so it goes cold between escalations. A warm 8.8 ms call becomes about 23 ms, and escalated frames hit about 38 ms p99 at 30 fps.
  • Fixes that failed: keep-warm made escalations queue behind the in-flight dummy pass. Micro-batching never formed batches at a 10% rate (mean batch 1.0–1.1), so its wait was pure added latency.
  • What won on the GPU: FP16 on every frame keeps the GPU warm and beat every routing variant on p99 and accuracy. Deadline-aware routing was the only fix that trimmed the tail, and it costs accuracy exactly when deadlines are tight.
  • Why that led to CPU-only: the winning process holds torch + MPS + two models in unified memory, about 1,010 MB. So Phase 3 asks how small a CPU-only path can get.

Online replay: p50 / p99 (ms), 10% escalation threshold

Source: results/stream/stream_results.csv · medians over clean repeats (health-check filtered) · 600 frames per run
Talking points: Phase 2
  • I built the router as a real streaming pipeline (one thread per stage, bounded queues, drop policy) to find out where the 33.9 ms tail came from.
  • I measured before fixing: warm vs idle GPU, CPU contention (ruled out), and four keep-warm strategies (only full forward passes help).
  • Number to emphasize: 8.8 ms warm vs about 23 ms after 50 ms idle. The GPU cold start is the tail.
  • I also found and fixed two harness bugs: macOS woke the replay thread 4–5 ms late, and ORT's default 8 threads spilled onto efficiency cores (p50 13.2 → 10.4 ms).
  • The conclusion is hardware-specific: on this Mac, run FP16 on every frame. Routing only pays when the GPU is unavailable, shared or power-limited.
Likely question: "Why not just keep the GPU warm?"
Answer: I tried four ways. Only a full dummy forward pass keeps it warm, and then a real request has to wait for that dummy to finish, so p99 didn't improve. It also adds CPU dispatch load at 60 fps.

Source: results/lean/bench_results.csv (median of 3 isolated processes, full 10,000 test set) · reference row from results/lean/stream_compare.csv (30 fps replay, 600 frames)

The four techniques

1 · Aligned heads

A ridge map (768 → 512) sends a cheaper encoder's features (lower resolution or fewer layers) to the full FP32 CLIP embedding of the same image, fit on 5,000 unlabeled train images. The frozen text embeddings still classify zero-shot.

Without it, layer-10 features give chance (10%); with it, 82.2%.

2 · Quantization-aware alignment

Fit that map on the quantized trunk's own features, so it also undoes quantization drift in the embedding space.

INT4 82.6% → 86.4%; INT8-dyn reaches 89.1% (FP32: 88.4%).

3 · Shared-weight resolution cascade

The ONNX trunk takes the position-embedding table as an input, so one session (one copy of the weights) runs at any resolution. Run at 128 px; re-run at 224 px only when the margin is low.

p50 10.4 → 5.2 ms for the same INT8 weights.

4 · numpy preprocessing

Bicubic resize is linear and separable, so OpenCV's exact resize matrices are precomputed and applied as two matmuls. That removes OpenCV from the process.

Base process RSS 74 → 50 MB, same latency.
Talking points: Phase 3
  • The goal: the lowest RAM and latency for online zero-shot inference, CPU only, with no fine-tuning of the encoder.
  • Number to emphasize: 182 MB vs 1,010 MB (cascade vs torch + MPS router) at 88.4% vs 86.7% accuracy.
  • The memory win comes from dropping torch and the GPU model; the accuracy win comes from quantization-aware alignment. They're separate levers that stack.
  • The cascade halves the median but adds a tail of about 16 ms on re-run frames. If p99 matters most, single-pass INT8 at 224 px has the tightest tail.
  • INT4 is the RAM floor (171 MB), but only with accuracy_level=4; default INT4 dequantizes to FP32 and is as slow as FP32.
Likely question: "Isn't 32×32 CIFAR flattering the low-resolution path?"
Answer: Yes, and I say so. Upscaled 32×32 images make 128 px unusually cheap, and native-resolution camera frames would gain less. The next step is validating on real frames, and a distilled small encoder trained to the aligned target.
